passage: Imagine a cinema that sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub at a modest price and a large tub at nearly twice that. Most customers buy the small one, until the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub priced only slightly below the large. Hardly anyone buys the medium, yet sales of the large tub rise sharply, so that the new option has done its work without ever being chosen. It exists to make the large tub look like a bargain, and in many such cases it succeeds; marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it produces turns up often enough, with magazine subscriptions, holiday packages and software plans as well as snacks, to deserve a more careful explanation than the claim that customers are easily fooled.

The standard account of choice in economics assumes that a person arrives at a shop with a ranking of the available goods already settled, and that the shop merely reveals it. On that account the decoy should be inert: if I prefer the small tub to the large one, the arrival of a medium tub that I do not want should leave my ranking of the other two untouched. What the decoy suggests instead is that many preferences are not retrieved but assembled on the spot, from the comparisons the menu makes easy. The medium tub is easy to compare with the large, being the same product at almost the same price with visibly less popcorn, whereas the comparison between the small and the large, which requires trading money against quantity, is considerably harder. Consequently, people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one.

It would be a mistake to conclude that preferences are endlessly pliable, for the effect is strongest when buyers are unsure what they want and have little experience of the product; a regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat is rarely moved. It also weakens when the decoy is so plainly inferior that customers notice the trick, and resentment at being steered can push them the other way. These limits matter, because they show that the decoy exploits a gap in knowledge rather than a defect of reason: constructing a preference out of whatever comparisons are available is a perfectly sensible strategy for someone who lacks better information.

The more interesting lesson concerns the menu itself. We usually treat the set of options as neutral background and the decision as the thing to be explained, but the decoy shows that the background is part of the decision. Whoever arranges the options, whether a cinema, a software firm setting its subscription tiers or a restaurant pricing its wine list, is not merely displaying choices but helping to form them. This does not make every arrangement sinister, since some arrangement is unavoidable, but it does mean that the question of what people chose cannot be separated from the question of what they were shown.

options.A: the menu contains more than three options, so that no single comparison stands out.
options.B: the products on the menu are expensive, so that customers take more care over every comparison they make.
options.C: buyers already know from experience what they want, or when the decoy is obviously inferior.
options.D: the product on sale is cheap and bought on impulse, like the popcorn sold in a cinema.

passage: When a painting sells at auction for a sum that would fund a hospital, two responses compete for the headlines. The first treats the price as a verdict: the market, pooling the judgements of many informed buyers, has declared this one of the most important works of its kind. The second treats it as a scandal: the sum has nothing to do with art and everything to do with vanity, speculation and the search for places to park wealth. Each response captures something, but both share a mistaken premise, which is that the price is either a measure of artistic value or a measure of nothing at all.

A price measures what someone will pay to own a thing, and owning a painting is not the same as valuing it as a painting. The buyer acquires an object that is unique, that cannot be reproduced without losing the very property being purchased, and that carries a name capable of conferring distinction on whoever holds it. Each of these features has a market logic of its own. Scarcity helps explain why a minor work by a celebrated painter can outsell a masterpiece by an obscure one; the name explains why a newly accepted attribution can multiply a canvas's price overnight without a single brushstroke changing. In neither case has anyone's experience of looking at the picture altered.

This does not mean that prices float free of critical judgement. Over long periods, the artists whom critics, historians and museums take seriously tend also to be the ones whose works command high prices, and it would be perverse to call this coincidence. But the connection runs largely through reputation rather than through the works themselves: esteem builds a name, the name creates demand, and demand sets the price. The market thus registers critical judgement at second hand, much as a credit rating registers a company's prospects without being the same thing as its earnings.

The real danger lies in the return journey. Once prices are reported as verdicts, they begin to shape the judgements they supposedly reflect. Visitors crowd around the record-breaking canvas while the room beside it stands empty; institutions hesitate to show or lend works whose insurance values have become unmanageable; young artists learn which styles sell. A measure of ownership, mistaken for a measure of worth, ends by teaching people what to look at. Resisting that confusion requires nothing more radical than remembering what a price is the price of.

options.A: illustrate how one thing can track another at second hand while remaining a different kind of thing.
options.B: warn that the art market, like the market for company debt, is liable to sudden collapses in value.
options.C: suggest that auction prices are as carefully calculated by experts as the ratings given to companies.
options.D: argue that buying paintings is a sounder investment than lending money to companies with good ratings.

passage: Every entrenched constitution invites an awkward question. If a majority of citizens today wishes to change some arrangement, why should it be prevented from doing so by rules that were drafted generations ago by people who are now dead, and who could not have imagined the conditions under which their successors live? A requirement that amendments win two-thirds of the legislature, or the approval of most regions, looks from this angle like a device for letting the past outvote the present. The objection has a democratic edge that is hard to dismiss: it asks by what right one generation sets the terms on which another must govern itself. Nor is it answered by praising the wisdom of the framers, since wisdom about one century is no warrant for authority over the next.

The most familiar answer appeals to self-binding. Just as a sailor who knows he will be tempted by a dangerous song may order his crew to tie him to the mast and ignore his later pleas, a people may bind itself in a calm moment against the passions it expects to feel in an agitated one. Entrenchment, on this account, is not the past overruling the present but the present protecting itself from its own worst impulses. The image is attractive, but it does not fit the case. The sailor binds himself, and the man who later strains at the ropes is the same man who gave the order. A constitution binds people who were not present when it was adopted and who gave no order at all. To call this self-binding is to assume precisely the continuity of the collective self that the objection calls into question.

A better defence starts from a different picture of what entrenchment does. Amendment rules do not, in practice, pit the living against the dead, because the dead cast no votes. What such rules do is set the terms on which living citizens must settle disagreements among themselves. When an amendment fails for want of a supermajority, it is defeated not by its framers but by a present minority large enough to block it. The requirement thus protects groups that might otherwise be outvoted on matters basic to their standing, and it encourages proposals that can attract support beyond a single faction. The protection is not merely theoretical: a group that knows it can block changes to its basic standing has less reason to fear the ordinary swings of electoral fortune, and more reason to accept defeat on everything else. Seen this way, the hand that restrains the majority is a living hand, and the real question is whether present minorities deserve such a veto, not whether the past deserves obedience.

This reframing does not make the original worry vanish. It succeeds only where amendment is demanding but genuinely possible. A constitution whose amendment procedure is so onerous that no change has been achieved in living memory, or which declares certain provisions unamendable altogether, really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after; there, no present coalition, however broad, can alter the text. The objection from the dead hand is therefore best understood not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes. Between a constitution that any passing majority may rewrite and one that no one can, the useful argument concerns how much agreement change should require, and that is a question each generation is entitled to keep asking.

options.A: A constitution's amendment rules were drafted by framers who could not have foreseen the conditions under which citizens now live.
options.B: An amendment backed by a narrow majority of citizens fails because a large regional minority votes against it.
options.C: A constitution requires two-thirds of the legislature and the approval of most regions for any amendment, and amendments have passed only rarely.
options.D: A provision declared permanently unamendable continues to bind citizens even though nearly all of them now wish to change it.

passage: Few words in journalism are now used with as much suspicion as objectivity. To its critics it names a pose: the pretence that reporters, alone among human beings, can step outside their own experience and describe the world from nowhere in particular. Put that way, the ideal is plainly impossible, and the critics are right to reject it. But it is worth asking whether that is the ideal anyone ever seriously defended. In at least one influential strand of its history, objectivity was proposed not as a description of the journalist but as a remedy for the journalist's limitations. Precisely because reporters could not be trusted to be neutral, the argument ran, they needed a method that would restrain what their partiality could do to the record.

The method in question resembled, in a modest way, the procedures of empirical inquiry. A claim was to be checked against more than one source; documents were to be preferred to recollection; and the reporter was to say where each piece of information came from, so that a reader or a rival could test it. On this understanding the objectivity belonged to the procedure, not to the person, much as a laboratory's results are trusted not because its scientists lack ambitions but because their work is arranged so that others can repeat it. A reporter with strong opinions could practise the method; indeed, the method existed for such reporters, since a reporter without opinions, if one could be found, would hardly need it.

What happened over the following decades was a quiet substitution. The discipline of verification, which is laborious and often invisible to the reader, was gradually overshadowed by a set of outward signs that were easier to display: a flat tone, a reluctance to draw conclusions, the habit of pairing every assertion with a counter-assertion. These signs were meant to signal fairness, but they could be produced without any verification at all. A story could quote two officials making incompatible claims, check neither, and still look objective. The appearance had detached itself from the practice it was supposed to indicate, and in some cases it obstructed that practice, since a reporter who had established that one of the officials was wrong was discouraged from saying so.

Much of the current attack on objectivity is in fact an attack on this degraded form, and to that extent it is justified. Where it goes wrong is in the alternative it sometimes proposes. If the remedy for false neutrality is for journalists to report openly from their convictions, readers are left to choose among the convictions of different reporters with no common procedure by which to test any of them. The proposal also concedes too much to the degraded form, accepting that objectivity simply is the flat tone and the paired quotation, and then discarding the whole inheritance on that basis. Candour about one's commitments is a virtue, but it is not a substitute for evidence; a frank partisan who has not checked the facts is no more reliable than a disguised one.

It should be conceded that method does not solve everything. Verification governs how a story is reported, not which stories are chosen, and the choice of what to investigate remains shaped by the interests and blind spots of those who make it. No procedure can remove that influence, and a newsroom that believes its method has made it neutral will be blind to it. Yet the concession limits the claim rather than defeating it. The case for objectivity understood as method is not that it makes journalism impartial but that it makes journalism answerable: it allows a reader who suspects a report to find out where it came from and whether it holds.

options.A: Objectivity as a checkable method rather than personal neutrality remains worth defending, though much criticism fairly targets a debased form of it.
options.B: Objectivity is valuable because a disciplined method of verification allows newsrooms to become impartial in choosing their stories.
options.C: Objectivity was always an impossible pose, and journalists should replace it by stating their own commitments openly to readers.
options.D: Objectivity declined because reporters abandoned the flat tone and balanced quotation that had once made their fairness visible to readers.

passage: The phrase 'guilty pleasure' has become one of the most common ways of talking about taste. A person confesses to loving a televised singing contest, a formulaic romance series or a song that dominated the charts in her teens, and the confession is offered with a smile that asks to be forgiven. On the surface the phrase is modest, even self-deprecating; looked at more closely, it does a surprising amount of work, and not all of that work is modest.

Consider what the speaker gains. By calling the pleasure guilty, she is able to enjoy the thing while signalling that she knows it is beneath her; she occupies the position of the enthusiast and the position of the critic at once. The confession is a kind of insurance: if her listener turns out to share the enthusiasm, nothing is lost; if the listener sneers, she has already sneered first. What looks like an admission of bad taste is therefore, very often, a display of good taste, since only someone who knows the rankings can confess to violating them.

This is why the phrase, for all its apparent humility, tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question. Every guilty pleasure implies an innocent one, a set of books, films and songs that may be enjoyed without apology because they are approved. The confession leaves that ranking intact; indeed it needs the ranking in order to mean anything. And the ranking itself is rarely examined. It is striking how often the pleasures labelled guilty are those associated with audiences who have little cultural prestige, the teenage, the provincial, the domestic, while the pleasures of the already respected are seldom described in this way, however predictable they may be.

It does not follow that no pleasure should ever make us uneasy. Some enjoyments really do deserve scrutiny: laughter at another person's humiliation, for instance, or the thrill of watching real suffering staged for entertainment. But in those cases the unease concerns what the pleasure does or endorses, not where its object sits in a ranking of prestige, and the honest response is to ask what we are enjoying and why. That question is worth asking of the singing contest as well. Perhaps the answer will be that it offers something real, the spectacle of ordinary people attempting something difficult in public. If so, the pleasure needs no apology; if not, a shrug and a smile will not settle the matter either.

options.A: Habitually confessing a pleasure as guilty is found, over time, to make people rate that work as highly as the approved ones.
options.B: The works that are most often called guilty pleasures turn out in fact to be associated mainly with audiences of very little cultural prestige.
options.C: Many people who use the phrase do so without any conscious wish to display their own good taste to others.
options.D: Some enjoyments, such as laughing at another person's humiliation, really do deserve to make us uneasy.

passage: We tend to think of the weekend as a natural feature of the calendar, as if two days of rest had always followed five of work. In fact the arrangement is fairly recent, and its history suggests that free time is not simply the absence of work but something that has to be made, defended and shaped. Before the factory, many artisans worked in bursts, labouring late into the night to finish an order and then taking a day or two off whenever it suited them; in parts of England the habit of stretching Sunday's rest into Monday was common enough to be given a mock saint's name, 'Saint Monday'.

Factory production could not tolerate this irregularity. Machines were expensive and had to run whenever the hands were present, and an employer could not plan production around workers who might drift in on Tuesday, so the long struggle over hours was therefore also a struggle over the shape of time. Workers wanted fewer hours; employers wanted predictable ones. The compromise that eventually emerged, first a half-day on Saturday and later the whole of it, gave each side part of what it sought. Workers won rest that was guaranteed rather than snatched, and employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.

It would be wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory. For most working people, guaranteed free time was a real gain, and it was won against resistance. But the weekend also changed what free time was. Leisure that had once been taken at the worker's discretion became a fixed block, the same for everyone, and a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to. Football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday, and leisure came increasingly to mean something one went out and paid for at a scheduled time.

The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better; it was often tied to poverty, to insecurity and to binges of overwork that left people exhausted. It is that arguments about working hours are never only about quantity. When people today argue over flexible schedules or a four-day week, they are reopening a question that the industrial age settled in one particular way: not merely how much time should be free, but who decides when it falls and what it is for.

options.A: Musicians who rested whenever bookings dried up join an orchestra with a fixed August holiday, and travel firms begin selling August trips to its players.
options.B: A town council turns a disused railway yard into a public park so that residents have somewhere to spend their free afternoons.
options.C: A company abolishes its fixed holiday calendar and allows staff to take leave whenever they choose, provided that their work is done on time.
options.D: Workers in a factory strike for higher wages and win a large raise, though their daily hours of work stay exactly as they were.

passage: Give a group of people an ordinary object, a coffee mug, say, or a pen, and then ask them how much they would accept to sell it; ask another group, who were not given the object, how much they would pay to acquire one. In experiments of this kind the sellers' prices have repeatedly been found to exceed the buyers' by a wide margin, even though the two groups were formed at random and there is no reason to think that the owners care more for mugs. Merely owning a thing, it seems, makes it more valuable to its owner. The finding has come to be known as the endowment effect, and it has become one of the best-known results in behavioural economics.

The standard interpretation explains it by loss aversion. People, on this view, evaluate outcomes not in absolute terms but as gains and losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Once the mug is mine, giving it up registers as a loss, whereas acquiring it, for someone who does not own it, registers only as a gain, and since the loss weighs more heavily, the owner demands more in compensation than the non-owner will pay. The account is economical, and it connects the mug experiments with a wide range of other behaviour, from the reluctance of investors to sell shares that have fallen in value to the stubbornness with which people defend entitlements they have only recently acquired.

A rival interpretation treats the gap as, at least in part, an artefact of the way such experiments are conducted. Participants who have never sold anything in a laboratory may be unsure what is being asked, may suspect that the experimenter knows the object's true value, or may simply apply a rule from everyday life, never to sell for less than it would cost to replace the thing. When procedures are altered so that participants practise the bidding mechanism and understand that misstating their values cannot help them, some studies have found the gap to shrink considerably. Supporters of this view also point out that professional traders, who buy and sell as a matter of routine, appear to show much less of the effect in the goods they deal in.

Each interpretation captures something real, and the dispute is less sharp than it is sometimes made to appear. The traders' case is telling not because it refutes loss aversion but because it suggests where loss aversion applies. A dealer who holds a stock of mugs holds them in order to sell them; parting with one is the purpose of having it, and so it does not register as a loss. A person who has been given a mug to use is in a different position, because the mug has already become, in a small way, part of her possessions, and parting with it means giving something up rather than completing a transaction. On this reading, what matters is not ownership as such but the frame in which a thing is held, as something to use or as something to exchange.

That reading has consequences beyond the laboratory. It implies that the gap between buying and selling prices is not a fixed constant of human nature, to be entered into economic models as a permanent correction, but a variable that depends on how people come to think of what they have. Markets that encourage people to regard their possessions as stock, as resale platforms arguably do, may weaken the effect; arrangements that encourage people to regard what they hold as their own, as long trial periods for products arguably do, may strengthen it. Whether either tendency is desirable is a separate question. The point is that the endowment effect, properly understood, is less a fact about objects or owners than a fact about the relation between them.

options.A: A bicycle shop owner asked to sell one of the identical bicycles displayed in the showroom.
options.B: A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them months ago, which their child has ridden every day since.
options.C: A student who bought a bicycle on a resale platform last week, planning to sell it on again for a profit.
options.D: A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them an hour ago, still unpacked, which they have not yet decided whether to keep.

passage: Discussions of social capital commonly distinguish two kinds of tie. Bonding ties link people who are alike in some respect that matters to them, such as kinship, faith, neighbourhood or trade, and they supply loyalty and mutual help. Bridging ties link people across such lines, and they supply information, opportunities and the habit of dealing with strangers. Having drawn the distinction, many writers proceed to rank the two. Bridging is cast as the civic virtue that open societies need; bonding is regarded with suspicion, as the stuff of cliques, favouritism and inward-looking communities. The ranking is attractive partly because it flatters an ideal of openness, and partly because the dangers of tight-knit groups are so easy to picture, whereas their quieter contributions rarely make news.

The ranking is too quick. Consider a family that moves to a city where it knows no one except a handful of people from its home district. Those people find it a room, lend it money, explain which offices to visit and which employers pay on time. They are bonding ties in the purest sense, and without them the family might never acquire the stability from which wider contacts become possible. The first job outside the community, or the first friendship with a neighbour of a different background, frequently comes through someone who was met by way of the close circle. In such cases bonding is not the rival of bridging but its precondition.

It does not follow that close groups are always benign. The same density of ties that allows a community to support its members allows it to watch them, and the help it offers can come with a demand for conformity: marry within, trade within, think as we do. A young woman who wishes to train for an occupation the group disapproves of may find that the network which once sustained her family now stands in her way, and that the price of leaving it is the loss of everything it provided. Here the closeness that was a resource becomes a closure.

What separates the two cases is not the strength of the bonding ties but their permeability: whether membership of the close group is compatible with forming ties outside it, or is made conditional on refusing them. A policy that tried to weaken community networks in the name of integration would therefore risk destroying the very support that allows newcomers to reach beyond those networks in the first place. A better question to ask of any close group is not how tightly it binds but whether it lets its members go.

options.A: They can be created reliably by public policies that weaken networks within communities.
options.B: They are often formed through contacts that bonding ties first make available to a person.
options.C: They are less valuable than bonding ties, which deserve the civic esteem that writers usually give to bridging.
options.D: They are formed mainly by people who do not belong to any close group of their own.

passage: Few facts about music are more familiar, or more puzzling on reflection, than the willingness of listeners to seek out music that makes them sad. People do not, on the whole, go looking for grief or disappointment in the rest of life, and they would think it odd to be offered a sorrowful afternoon as a treat. Yet slow laments, songs of loss and the darker movements of symphonies are among the most loved music in many traditions, and listeners return to them deliberately.

One response dissolves the puzzle by denying its premise. On this view the listener does not really feel sad at all; she recognises sadness in the music, much as she might recognise a sorrowful expression on a carved mask, and what she enjoys is the beauty and skill with which the sadness is expressed. The view has the merit of explaining why sad music does not ruin anyone's day. But it fits poorly with what many listeners report, which is that they are moved, sometimes to tears, and not merely informed. A second response accepts that the feeling is real and explains the pleasure by the frame around it: the sadness arrives without a loss to cause it and without consequences to follow, so it can be savoured in a way that the sadness of life cannot.

Both responses capture something, but both treat the emotion as a single state, present or absent, mild or intense. What music does with an emotion is closer to giving it a shape over time. A lament does not simply announce sorrow; it gathers, rises, breaks, returns to a phrase heard earlier and comes to rest. The listener who follows it is led through a version of sorrow that has a beginning, an end and a recognisable order, which is precisely what the sorrows of ordinary life usually lack. The pleasure, on this account, lies less in the feeling than in the form the feeling is given.

This does not mean that sad music always pleases, or pleases everyone. Many people who are grieving find that they cannot listen to the music they loved before, at least for a time, and their experience is a useful check on any theory. A frame that keeps sadness at a safe distance should make such music easier to bear in grief, not harder. The account offered here does better: a shaped and completed sorrow may be unbearable to someone whose own sorrow has no shape yet, because the contrast is too sharp.

options.A: The frame view correctly predicts that people in grief will find sad music harder to bear than before.
options.B: The view that listeners only recognise sadness can explain why sad music does not spoil a listener's day.
options.C: On the frame view, the sadness of music can be savoured because no loss causes it and no consequences follow.
options.D: A lament may return to a phrase heard earlier in the piece before it finally comes to rest.

passage: Philosophical discussions of ethics characteristically concentrate on the moment of decision. A situation is described, the available options are set out, and the question is which of them a good person would choose. This framing is natural for the purposes of argument, but it quietly assumes that the morally significant work begins only once the situation has been described. In ordinary life, nobody hands us the description. What we take the situation to be, which features stand out and which recede into the background, is settled largely by what we attend to, and that settling is accomplished before any choice is considered.

Consider a manager who prides herself on her fairness. When a request for leave arrives, she weighs it conscientiously against the requirements of the team, and she applies identical rules to everyone. Yet for months she has failed to notice that one reserved employee has grown withdrawn and anxious, while she registered immediately when a more assertive colleague appeared dissatisfied. Her decisions, examined individually, may be beyond reproach. The defect lies upstream, in a pattern of attention that has made some people's difficulties vivid to her and rendered others' invisible.

It may be objected that this demands too much of ordinary moral agents. Noticing is not something we do at will; we cannot be blamed for failing to perceive what never came to our notice, any more than for failing to hear a sound pitched too high for human ears. There is something genuinely correct in the objection. No single lapse of attention is a choice, and it would be unjust to treat it as though it were. But attention is not fixed in the way the range of hearing is. It is formed by what we have habitually looked for, by whom we have taken seriously, and by the stories we tell ourselves about the people around us, and these are things over which, across time, we have considerable influence.

The upshot is that moral improvement is frequently less a matter of resolving to choose better than of learning to see better. A person who wishes to be fair must ask not only whether her decisions follow sound principles but also whose circumstances reach her as calls for decision at all. This is slower and less dramatic work than heroic choice, and it rarely earns admiration, since what it changes is largely invisible from outside. It is nonetheless where a great deal of moral life actually takes place.

options.A: Someone may be answerable for a failure to notice even if that particular failure was not something she chose.
options.B: Because attention is shaped by habit, each single lapse of attention deserves the same blame as a deliberately bad decision.
options.C: Moral improvement consists solely in learning to see better and never in learning to choose better.
options.D: Since changes in attention are invisible from outside, they cannot be judged morally by other people.

passage: It has become a commonplace that rewarding people for doing what they already enjoy can make them enjoy it less. Picture a child who draws for the pleasure of it and is then promised a prize for each picture. While the prizes continue, the drawing may increase. When they stop, the child may draw less than before the prizes began, as though the activity had been converted from play into work and then left unpaid. The phenomenon is real, and it has been reproduced often enough to deserve to be taken seriously. What is less often noticed is how many conditions it depends upon, and how quickly it fades when they are absent.

The effect appears most reliably when the reward is tangible, expected in advance and given for doing the task rather than for doing it well. A prize announced beforehand and handed over for every picture invites the child to understand the drawing as a means to the prize. An unexpected treat, by contrast, cannot have been the reason for drawing, and praise that tells the child something about the quality of the work may even strengthen interest, since it feeds the sense of competence that made the activity enjoyable in the first place. The same physical reward can therefore have opposite effects depending on what it communicates to the person who receives it.

Equally important, the effect presupposes that there was interest to undermine. Many tasks that people are paid or rewarded for, from sorting files to practising scales, hold little intrinsic appeal at the outset, and for these, rewards cannot crowd out an enjoyment that was never there. Indeed, a reward may keep someone at a dull task long enough for skill to grow and for the task itself to become absorbing, so that interest arrives because of the incentive rather than in spite of it.

The sensible conclusion lies between two slogans. Those who say that rewards destroy motivation generalise from a narrow set of conditions; those who say that people simply do whatever they are paid to do ignore the conditions entirely. The better question in any particular case is how the reward is likely to be read: as an attempt to control behaviour that would otherwise not occur, or as information about how well something is being done. The first reading tends to erode interest in activities that people already value; the second tends to support it.

options.B: removes the child's expectation that drawing will be rewarded again in the future.
options.C: comes unexpectedly and so cannot have been the child's reason for drawing.
options.D: is less tangible than a prize and so is harder for the child to treat as a payment.

passage: The most familiar complaint about recommendation algorithms is that they trap each of us in a private enclosure. Because a system learns what a user has clicked, watched or bought, the argument runs, it will keep offering more of the same, until every listener hears only the music that confirms their existing taste and every reader meets only the opinions they already hold. On this picture the danger is fragmentation: a public that once shared a common stock of songs, books and news splinters into millions of sealed niches, each tuned to one person.

The complaint is not baseless, but it may have the main tendency of these systems the wrong way round. Most recommendation engines do not learn from one user in isolation; they learn from the aggregate behaviour of very large numbers of users, and they rank items partly by how much engagement those items have already attracted. That design creates a feedback loop. An item that gets a slight early lead is shown to more people, which earns it more engagement, which earns it still more prominence. Imagine two songs of equal appeal released on the same day, one of which happens to be picked up by a few enthusiastic listeners in its first hours. Under such a loop the small, accidental difference can harden into an enormous gap, and the second song may effectively disappear, not because anyone judged it worse but because no one was shown it.

If this is right, the characteristic risk is less fragmentation than concentration: attention pooling ever more heavily on a few items, while the vast catalogue that digital distribution made available sits largely unvisited. The early hope that online platforms would let obscure work find its small audiences depended on people actually encountering that work, and a ranking system that rewards prior popularity makes such encounters rarer than the size of the catalogue suggests.

It would be wrong to present this as something algorithms invented. Bestseller lists, radio playlists and the front tables of bookshops have always amplified what was already selling, and cultural markets have long been marked by a few large successes and many neglected works. What is new is the speed of the loop and its invisibility. A bookseller choosing what to display is a person whose choices can be questioned; a ranking produced by continuous automated feedback appears simply to report what people want, when it is partly manufacturing it. The remedy, if there is one, lies less in protecting users from their own tastes than in asking how much of what looks like popular demand is an echo of earlier exposure.

options.A: It would remove popularity from rankings entirely, since amplifying success is a harm peculiar to algorithms.
options.B: It would aim chiefly at showing users fewer of the items that match the tastes they have already displayed.
options.C: It would ask whether apparent popularity shows real preference or just the prominence an item had earlier.
options.D: It would be achieved once automated rankings were made as slow to respond as the choices of booksellers.

passage: Why should anyone help a stranger they will never meet again? Kindness between relatives can be explained by shared interests, and kindness between neighbours by the expectation that favours will be returned. But much of human cooperation takes place between people who are neither kin nor repeat partners: the traveller who returns a lost wallet, the customer who corrects an undercharge. One influential answer is that such acts are paid for not by the person helped but by everyone who comes to hear of them. If people prefer to help those who have a record of helping others, then a good reputation is an asset, and an act of generosity towards a stranger is an investment in it. Biologists call this arrangement indirect reciprocity.

The idea has an obvious weakness, and its defenders have had to work hard to answer it. Reputation is only as useful as the information that carries it. In a small band where everyone watches everyone, deeds are seen and remembered; in a large society most of them go unwitnessed. Here language does decisive work. Gossip, often dismissed as idle, is the channel through which a person's conduct becomes known to people who never saw it, and a great deal of everyday conversation consists of exactly this exchange of judgements about absent third parties. Without such talk, indirect reciprocity could hardly operate beyond the scale of a village.

A subtler problem concerns the judgements themselves. Suppose I refuse to help someone who is known to cheat. Should observers count my refusal against me? If they do, anyone who withholds help from cheats will be punished for it, and cheating becomes safer. If they do not, observers must keep track not only of what people did but of whom they did it to and why. Models of indirect reciprocity suggest that cooperation is far more stable under the second, more demanding standard, which may help explain why people care so much about motives and context when they assess one another's behaviour.

It would be too much to say that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers. People sometimes behave generously in conditions of genuine anonymity, and laboratory attempts to show that subtle cues of being watched, such as pictures of eyes, make people more generous have produced mixed results. A defender of the reputational account can reply that habits formed in a world where anonymity was rare are not switched off merely because a particular situation happens to be unobserved. That reply is plausible, but it shifts the explanation from calculation to disposition, and it should be acknowledged as a shift. What survives is a narrower and more defensible claim: that the expectation of being talked about is one of the main forces that make large-scale cooperation possible, and that it works only as well as the talk is accurate.

options.A: carries news of a person's conduct to people who were not present and never witnessed it.
options.B: allows relatives and neighbours to coordinate the return of favours that they owe to one another.
options.C: replaces the need to judge other people's motives with a simple record of who helped whom.
options.D: discourages people from cheating by making them fear immediate punishment from those who watched them.

options.C: Reputation fully explains cooperation among strangers once the spread of gossip and the careful judging of motives are taken into account.
options.D: Indirect reciprocity cannot work in large societies, because observers cannot judge whether refusing to help a cheat is wrong.

passage: Two stories are told about the anger that seems to pervade online discussion, and each is convenient for someone. In the first, the ranking systems that decide what appears in a feed have manufactured outrage, turning otherwise reasonable people into combatants. In the second, told chiefly by those who build such systems, a feed merely reflects its users: it shows people what they engage with, and if what they engage with is furious, the fault lies in human nature, not in the code. The first story flatters users, who become the victims of a machine; the second flatters engineers, who become the neutral servants of a public. Neither is quite right.

Against the first story, it must be granted that outrage is old. Pamphleteers, broadsheets and street-corner orators discovered long before any computer that indignation sells, and audiences have always lingered over a scandal longer than over the correction that followed it. A ranking system that favours whatever holds attention did not invent this appetite. It found the appetite already there, and it could hardly have succeeded so quickly if it had not. Any account that treats the present climate as wholly unprecedented must therefore explain why the appetite it deplores appears so reliably in the commercial history of every earlier medium of mass communication.

But the second story trades on an ambiguity in the word 'want'. A feed ranked by engagement learns what people react to: what they click, what they pause over, what they reply to in anger. Reaction is not the same as endorsement. A person may linger over a provocative post in the way a driver slows to look at an accident, and may say, if asked afterwards, that she wishes she had seen less of such material. A system that learns only from the lingering will give her more of it, and will describe the result as giving her what she wants. It is giving her what she wanted in the moment of reaction, which may be the opposite of what she wants on reflection.

The older media of indignation differed in a further way that the mirror story overlooks. A newspaper editor chose what to print, but the feedback that reached him was slow and coarse, a matter of sales figures and letters to the editor. A feed reports, to every person who publishes in it, exactly how each post performed, often within minutes. Those who write for such an audience learn quickly which tone is rewarded, and many adjust accordingly, not because they are cynical but because they would like to be read. The ranking system therefore does not merely distribute a fixed supply of anger; it shapes the supply, by teaching producers what pays. A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror.

It does not follow that the remedy is simply to rank posts by what people say, on reflection, that they value. Reflective preferences are harder to measure, easier to misreport and, when a platform infers them, open to the charge that the platform has substituted its own judgement for the user's. These are real objections, and they counsel modesty about any redesign. But they cut both ways. A system that optimises for momentary reaction has also made a judgement about what its users really want; it has simply made that judgement silently, and in favour of the version of the user that is easiest to count. Neutrality, in this domain, is not an available option; the only choice is between an explicit conception of the user's interests and an implicit one.

options.A: defending the builders of ranking systems against critics who blame them for a feature of human nature.
options.B: proposing that platforms rank posts according to what users say, on reflection, that they value most.
options.C: arguing that engagement ranking neither invents outrage nor simply mirrors it, but amplifies and reshapes it.
options.D: demonstrating that ranking systems are the main cause of the anger that now characterises discussion online.

passage: Discussions of the so-called file drawer problem usually begin with journals. Editors, the complaint runs, prefer results that show something: a drug that works, an effect that appears, a difference between groups. Studies that find nothing are harder to place, and so they remain in researchers' filing cabinets while the published literature fills up with positive findings. A reader who surveys that literature will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print. The literature, in other words, is not a sample of the research that was done but a selection from it, made on the very quantity that readers most want to estimate.

There is truth in this account, and the remedy it suggests, journals that commit in advance to publishing well-conducted studies whatever they find, deserves the support it has received. But the account places the drawer in the wrong office. Ask a working scientist what became of her last inconclusive experiment and the answer is seldom that an editor turned it down. More often it was never written up at all. The study was abandoned before any journal had a chance to reject it, and it sits in the drawer because its own author put it there.

The reason is not laziness. A positive result, whatever its other defects, announces itself: something happened. A null result is mute about its own meaning. It may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol. The researcher who obtained it is often the person least able to tell which, and the most honest description she could offer, that she looked and did not see, is one that few colleagues would think worth the trouble of reading. Writing such a paper costs weeks and earns little, and the decision to move on is, from where she stands, entirely rational.

If this is right, obliging journals to accept null results treats the symptom at the far end. The drawer will empty only when null results become informative, and that depends on decisions made before any data are collected: samples large enough that a real effect would probably have been seen, procedures specified in advance so that a failure cannot be blamed afterwards on improvisation, checks built in to show that the apparatus was working. A null result obtained under such conditions says something definite, and researchers will publish it for the same reason they publish anything, because it tells their colleagues something they did not know.

options.A: editors have made it clear in advance that they will not consider studies that find no effect.
options.B: she is too occupied with newer projects to spend time on work that has already failed.
options.C: she fears that publishing it would contradict the published findings of senior colleagues in her field.
options.D: she herself often cannot tell what the absence of the expected effect actually means.

passage: Ask a collector why she keeps buying stamps, coins or toy cars long after there is any room left to display them, and the answer is rarely about the objects themselves. More often it concerns a gap: the one issue missing from a run, the single variant that would finish a set. Collecting, on this view, is less a love of things than a love of completion. The individual stamp matters because of the place it occupies in a series, and its value to the collector rises sharply as the series nears its end, often far beyond anything a buyer outside the hobby would think of paying.

Manufacturers learned long ago to exploit this. A cereal box that contains one of twelve plastic figures, a sticker album with a few deliberately scarce pages, a line of trading cards issued in waves: each turns an ordinary purchase into a step towards a whole that the buyer did not know he wanted until he was shown its outline. The empty album is the real product. Once its spaces are printed, every blank becomes a small reproach, and the purchase that fills it brings a satisfaction out of all proportion to what was bought.

It would be easy to conclude that collecting is simply a manufactured compulsion, a weakness that the market has learned to farm. That conclusion goes too far. Many of the most devoted collectors pursue series that no company ever designed: the railway timetables of a vanished line, the matchboxes of hotels that have since closed, the scattered editions of a minor poet. Here it is the collector who defines the set, deciding what counts as belonging to it and therefore what counts as missing. Such collecting is a way of ordering the world, of drawing a boundary around a scattered field and making it intelligible. Many museums began, in part, as exactly this kind of private project.

The difference between the two kinds of collecting is not the passion involved, which can be equally intense, but who holds the map. When the series is invented by a seller, completion is a target set by someone else, and the finish line is often moved just as it comes into view, with a new wave or a special edition. When the collector draws the map, completion is a judgement she makes for herself, and the pleasure lies as much in the defining as in the finding. The danger of the commercial version is not that it creates desire, since all collecting does that, but that it quietly takes the act of definition away from the person doing the collecting.

options.A: argue that collectors value the objects they gather for their beauty and rarity rather than for the places they fill in a set, whoever happens to have designed that set.
options.B: trace how private collections of timetables, matchboxes and editions gradually developed into the public museums of today, and to praise the collectors who began them.
options.C: show that collecting is a compulsion created by manufacturers, who profit by persuading buyers to complete sets that they never wanted until the empty spaces were shown to them.
options.D: distinguish collecting in which the collector defines the series from collecting in which a seller does, and to show that the latter's harm lies in removing that power.

passage: Few political promises are as widely shared as the promise of social mobility. Parties that agree on little else agree that a child's prospects should not be fixed by the circumstances of her birth, and the claim that mobility has stalled is one of the most damaging charges that can be laid against a government. Yet the word covers two quite different things, and much public argument about it goes astray because the two are run together.

The first is absolute mobility: the share of people who end up better off than their parents, whether by income or by the kind of work they do. The second is relative mobility: the extent to which a person's position in the distribution, as opposed to their standard of living, differs from their parents' position. The two can move independently. In a period of rapid growth and expanding professional employment, most children may outearn their parents and many may enter occupations their parents never held, even if the chance of a child born near the bottom reaching the top, compared with that of a child born near the top, has not changed at all. Everyone rides the escalator up, but the order of people on it stays the same.

This distinction explains a puzzle. When growth slows and the expansion of professional jobs levels off, absolute mobility falls, and people who do no better than their parents feel, reasonably enough, that something has closed. They often conclude that society has become less fair. Imagine a town where a mill employed one generation and new offices employed the next. The children did better than their parents without anyone being pushed aside, and the town experienced this as openness. When the offices stop hiring, the grandchildren find that the climb has ended. Yet on the measures that track their position against the children of the office managers, the chances may be much as they were: what has disappeared is not openness but the rising tide that once let a whole generation move up without anyone having to move down. The sense of closure is real; its diagnosis is frequently mistaken.

The distinction also exposes an awkwardness that politicians prefer to leave unspoken. Absolute mobility can, in principle, be enjoyed by everyone at once. Relative mobility cannot. If positions are ranked, then for one family to climb another must fall, and a serious commitment to relative mobility is therefore a commitment to downward mobility for some children of the comfortable. It is not surprising that the comfortable resist it, often without any sense of doing so, through the ordinary devices of private tuition, a well-placed word, or the purchase of a house near the right school. Each of these looks like ordinary care for one's own children; together they amount to a defence of position.

None of this makes one kind of mobility the real one. Absolute mobility answers a question about material progress: are people living better than their parents did? Relative mobility answers a question about fairness: does birth still decide where one ends up? Both questions matter, and neither is easy to answer with confidence, since incomes fluctuate and occupations change their meaning across generations. But a society that wants more of the second kind should be honest that it cannot be had at no one's expense, and a society that mourns the loss of the first should not mistake a slower economy for a more rigid one.

options.A: people born near the bottom rise faster than those born near the top whenever the economy is growing quickly.

passage: A respectable argument holds that negative criticism of new books is a waste of everyone's time. So many books are published each year that no critic can notice more than a sliver of them; the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious, and to spend it explaining why a book is bad is to deny it to a book that deserves attention. On this view the most damning verdict a critic can deliver is silence. A poor book left unmentioned simply sinks, and nothing is lost except the pleasure that some critics take in wounding. The position has the further appeal of seeming kind, which is no small recommendation in a literary world where writers and critics are often the same people.

The argument is tidy, but it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read. If that were so, the notice of a weak book would indeed be wasted, since a reader who is told merely to skip something has learned nothing that he could use elsewhere. But criticism has always done something besides sorting. A careful account of why a book fails is also an account of what success would have looked like, and in giving it the critic makes public a set of standards that readers can test, dispute and apply for themselves. The reader who follows a well-argued case against a novel he admired may end unconvinced, yet he will read the next novel more alertly.

There is a further cost to silence. If critics write only about the books they admire, praise becomes the sole currency of criticism, and like any currency issued without limit it loses its value. A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way. Readers soon learn to discount it, as they discount the admiring phrases printed on the cover of every new book, and the critic whose praise is sincere is then heard no more clearly than the publicist. The possibility of dispraise is what gives praise its meaning.

None of this licenses cruelty, and the case for restraint does have force in one kind of instance. A modest first novel from a small press, which few people will encounter anyway, gains nothing from a public demolition, and neither do its readers. The negative notice earns its space when the book in question is prominent: widely praised, heavily promoted, or likely to shape what others write. There the critic who dissents is not kicking someone who is down but contesting a reputation that is already shaping public taste, and that is among the most useful things criticism can do.

options.A: Critics take more pleasure in writing unfavourable notices than favourable ones.
options.B: A poor book that is ignored will sell fewer copies than one that is attacked in print.
options.C: Most of the books published each year are of poor quality and deserve no attention.
options.D: Criticism exists solely to help readers decide which books are worth their time.

passage: Two attitudes to the character of the speaker run through the study of persuasion, and they are hard to reconcile. The first, familiar from introductory logic, holds that an argument stands or falls on its own terms. Who makes it is irrelevant; to reject a claim because of the person advancing it is to commit a fallacy, and to accept a claim because of the person is the same error in a friendlier mood. The second attitude is older. Aristotle counted the character of the speaker among the means of persuasion, alongside appeals to the emotions of the audience and to the argument itself, and he did not present it as a regrettable weakness of listeners. A speaker who seems sensible, honest and well disposed towards the audience is, on this view, more worthy of belief, and an audience is right to take that into account.

The logician's attitude is correct for a particular situation: one in which the listener can examine the argument fully. A proof in geometry is no better for coming from a famous mathematician. But most of the claims on which people must act are not like proofs. A patient cannot check a diagnosis, a juror cannot repeat the forensic analysis, and a citizen cannot audit the statistics behind a policy. In such cases the listener is not choosing between evaluating the argument and evaluating the speaker; the argument is largely out of reach, and the speaker's record, competence and incentives are the best evidence available. To attend to them is not a lapse in reasoning but reasoning under a division of intellectual labour that no one can escape.

If this rehabilitates the appeal to character, it also shows where that appeal goes wrong. Credibility is earned in a domain. The physician's record is evidence about diagnoses, not about tax policy, and the honesty of a popular broadcaster is evidence that he reports what he believes, not that what he believes is true. Much modern persuasion works by carrying trust from the place where it was earned to a place where it has no bearing: the athlete who recommends an investment, the scientist who pronounces on matters far from her field. The listener who accepts such claims is not wrong to rely on character in general; she is wrong about which character she is relying on.

The two attitudes, then, are less opposed than they first appear. The logician is right that character cannot make a bad argument good, and the rhetorician is right that, where arguments cannot be inspected, character is often all a listener has to go on. What a careful audience needs is neither a rule against attending to the speaker nor a habit of trusting the likeable, but the narrower discipline of asking what, exactly, the speaker's credibility is credibility about.

options.A: reasoning soundly, since the judge's credibility was earned in the very domain the advice concerns.
options.B: justified only if the listener has first worked through all the legal reasoning behind the advice.
options.C: committing the fallacy that introductory logic warns against, since legal advice should be judged only on its merits.
options.D: relying on character improperly, since a long career shows sincerity rather than the truth of a belief.

passage: For a long time the sociology of taste worked with a simple map. At the top of the social order sat a refined culture of opera, poetry and the old masters, at the bottom sat popular entertainments, and a person's place in society could be read, with fair accuracy, from the position of their preferences on this ladder. Elites, on this picture, distinguished themselves by what they refused. Liking the wrong music was not merely a private failing but a mark of origin.

Surveys of cultural consumption in a number of wealthy countries have since complicated the map. The most educated and affluent groups, it turns out, are no longer best described as snobs who like only high culture. They are more often omnivores: they go to the opera and to the cinema, read literary fiction and crime novels, and are happy to discuss both a string quartet and a pop album. Some observers have greeted this as the end of cultural hierarchy, a sign that the old boundaries between high and low have dissolved and that taste has become a matter of individual preference rather than of class.

That conclusion is premature. Breadth of taste is itself unevenly distributed, because it requires money, time, travel and, above all, the confidence to move between worlds without feeling out of place. The person who can talk knowledgeably about both a symphony and a street-food stall has accumulated a cultural range that is far harder to acquire than a liking for either alone. Moreover, omnivores rarely consume popular forms in the same way as their usual audiences. They tend to approach them with a knowing, curatorial attitude, prizing a song for its place in the history of a genre or enjoying a film with a touch of irony, and this manner of liking can mark distance as effectively as refusal once did.

Nor is the omnivore's appetite unlimited. Research on what people say they dislike has suggested that the forms most often rejected by the highly educated tend to be those most associated with the least educated, so that the boundary has moved rather than vanished. None of this means that the loosening of old hierarchies is an illusion; it is a genuine change that the opera house must now compete for prestige with a well-chosen food truck. But distinction has not disappeared with the decline of snobbery. It has learned to express itself through openness, and openness is harder to criticise than exclusion because it looks so much like a virtue.

options.A: It shows that the old snobbery of paragraph 1 has returned among the highly educated in exactly its earlier form.
options.B: It introduces evidence showing that the omnivore pattern found in surveys is confined to a small number of wealthy countries and does not hold elsewhere.
options.C: It adds a further reason to doubt that hierarchy has ended, grants that real change has occurred, and then restates that distinction persists in a new form.
options.D: It withdraws the doubts raised in paragraph 3 by conceding that the loosening of cultural hierarchy is genuine after all.
